title: Python: names and objects
summary: A variable is a label on an object: why changing a list in a function changes it outside too.

text: In Python, a variable is a name stuck on an object, like a label.
- The list is the object. hosts is only its name.
- The = sign sticks a name on an object. It doesn't copy anything.
backup = hosts puts a second label on the same list.
- Change the list through one name, and the other name sees it too.
- print(backup) shows cache: there was never a second list.
To get a second list, ask for a copy.
- Now each name has its own list: changing one leaves the other alone.
- hosts[:] is a copy too; you'll see it in older code.
- copy() copies the list, not what's inside: lists inside it stay shared.
A function gets the same object, under a new name.
- xs.sort() or xs.remove(…) change the caller's list.
- Build a new list and return it instead: sorted(xs) returns a new, sorted list.
Some objects can never change: numbers, strings, tuples.
- .upper() doesn't change "sam": it makes a new string.
- So you must keep the result: name = name.upper().
- Lists and dicts can change in place: that's where shared labels surprise you.
